newsitem.title: USA: Wall St looks ready for Fed interest-rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Wall St looks ready for Fed interest-rate hike.

text.p: Less than 24 hours before a key Federal Reserve policy meeting, Wall Street appears to have discounted what would be the first interest-rate hike in more than two years.
The Federal Open Market Committee will meet on Tuesday to decide whether the time has come to tighten monetary policy to help sustain moderate economic growth.

In several appearances before Congress this year, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has gradually persuaded the financial markets that the central bank believes a rate hike would be a timely move to counter potential inflation pressures that could emerge by late this year or early next.

The latest batch of economic reports strengthened the argument for a pre-emptive move by the Fed to slow economic growth. Last week, the Commerce Department reported that builders broke ground on new homes and apartments in February at the fastest clip in nearly three years.

Stock and bond markets have sold off over the past few weeks in response to comments from Greenspan and other Fed officials. By now, the markets seem to have conditioned themselves to an interest rate boost.
Greenspan has repeatedly warned of the risks to inflation posed by tight labor markets while acknowledging that thus far, prices have remained well under control.

The clearest evidence that the markets have discounted a Fed rate hike -- the first increase since 1994 -- is that short-term Treasury bond rates, the sector most sensitive to official short-term interest rates, were unchanged on Monday.

Short-term bill rates have risen in the last month. Three-month rates ended at 5.02 percent on February 25, one day before Wall Street heard Greenspan deliver his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins to Congress in a decidedly hawkish tone.
On February 26, the day of the testimony, three-month bill rates rose to close at 5.05 percent and they have risen ever since. On Monday, the rates held steady at 5.26 percent.

"The fact that those rates have risen lately -- and pretty dramatically after Greenspan spoke last week -- certainly indicates that any people doubting that there would be a rate increase are not doubting any more," said Anthony O'Bryan, vice president and technical market analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

The Fed funds rate, a benchmark for other short-term rates that is the Fed's main lever for influencing the economy, now stands at 5.25 percent. Most of those forecasting a rate rate rise look for a modest increase of a quarter percentage point.
The last time the Fed raised rates was in February 1995, when it completed the last of a series of increases that resulted in a doubling of the funds rate during 1994 to 1995.
O'Bryan said U.S. financial markets "will rally after the (Fed rate hike) announcement (expected Tuesday afternoon) and might even rally ahead of it.

"Number one, it was an uncertainty that the market was dealing with and now it's gone," he said. "And at least from the point of view of bond investors, it would mean that Alan Greenspan is keeping his reputation as an inflation fighter and that should help the long-end of the curve."

Indeed, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was already up 8/32 to 95-31/32, yielding 6.95 percent, in early morning trading Monday. Last week, the long-term rate jumped to the 7 percent level for the first time since September of 1996.
A bond rally should help stocks, said O'Bryan.
"Typically, when bonds rally, stocks rally along with them," he said.

Foreign exchange markets were also adjusting to the idea of the central bank being in a tightening mode for the first time in two years. Analysts said currency players had priced in a 25-basis-point increase in the Federal funds rate to 5.50 percent, debating only when a second hike might come.
"The rate hike should be supportive for the dollar," said O'Bryan. "The dollar doesn't need any help, but the higher rates will help anyway."

Much of the financial markets' reaction to a Fed rate hike on Tuesday would depend on whether investors believe the increase is the first of many rate increases, the first of two or three such moves, or a single lonely shot fired in the dark against the specter of inflation, analysts said.

"Most people will conclude that it's the first of two moves and some are hedging in the direction of another rate tightening (at the next FOMC meeting) on May 20," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
On just one rate hike alone, the dollar could edge up to 170 versus the mark and to 124 against the yen, said Platt. The equity market, though, would be vulnerable to more selling, he said.
"I think the stock market could very easily drop another 150 points this week," he said.
"A lot of people in the stock market are still hoping that the Fed is not going to move even though it seems pretty obvious to bond market participants that the Fed is moving," said Platt.
But if opinion weighs in on the side of two or three rate increases, financial markets could see some sharper moves.

"The dollar will go to 173 marks and 126 yen if the rate increase is one of two or three moves and the stock market will go down 400 or 500 points (on the Dow Jones Industrial Average) from where we are now," said Platt.
In early afternoon trade, the Dow was up about six points to 6811.42.
A stock slide would not come all at once and not all of it would be attributable to higher rates, Platt said.

"The stock market would practice denial for awhile but clearly the bloom is off the rose (in the equity market)," said Platt. "The Nasdaq is in a major correctional move already and I think in the Dow, the Eastman Kodak announcement on Friday (that sales were weak in January and February) will be one of many disappointments."
As for the bond market, much will depend on upcoming economic data, Platt said.

"Right now the bond market is very much set to flatten the curve and push rates up on the two- and three-year maturities and keep the bond (yield) below seven percent," said Platt. "But the bond market needs the next wave of employment and inflation data to validate the flattening of the yield curve."
(( -- Ellen Freilich, North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
